q: A private limited company that is not a subsidiary or holding of a public company has paid-up capital plus reserves of Rs 90 lakh, total borrowings from banks of Rs 90 lakh at all points during the year, and total revenue of Rs 9 crore. Is CARO 2020 applicable?
o: Yes, revenue of Rs 9 crore crosses the CARO limit of Rs 5 crore
Yes, bank borrowings of Rs 90 lakh cross the Rs 50 lakh ceiling
No, the capital, borrowings and revenue limits are all satisfied here
No, but only because it is not a subsidiary of a public company
why: The private company exemption requires paid-up capital plus reserves not exceeding Rs 1 crore, borrowings not exceeding Rs 1 crore at any point in the year, and revenue not exceeding Rs 10 crore. All three limits are met here, so CARO does not apply. Revenue of Rs 9 crore is below the Rs 10 crore ceiling, not the Rs 5 crore figure used elsewhere.

q: Which of the following companies remains within the scope of CARO 2020?
o: A banking company as defined in the Banking Regulation Act 1949
A One Person Company as defined in Section 2(62) of the Act
A Section 8 company licensed to promote charitable objects
An unlisted public company with paid-up capital of Rs 40 lakh
why: CARO 2020 expressly excludes banking companies, insurance companies, Section 8 companies, One Person Companies and small companies. An unlisted public company is covered regardless of size because the private company thresholds do not apply to it.

q: Under CARO 2020 clause 3(i)(c), the auditor must comment on title deeds of immovable property not held in the name of the company. Which item is outside the scope of this comment?
o: A factory building disclosed under property, plant and equipment
A godown building held as investment property under Ind AS 40
A residential flat held as stock-in-trade by a real estate firm
Land as right-of-use asset under a duly executed lease deed
why: The clause covers immovable property whose title deeds are not in the company name, but expressly excludes properties where the company is the lessee and the lease agreement is duly executed in favour of the lessee. Investment property and stock-in-trade immovable property are within scope.

q: CARO 2020 clause 3(ii)(a) requires reporting on physical verification of inventory. The discrepancy threshold that triggers specific reporting is:
o: Discrepancies of 5 percent or more noticed for any class of inventory
Discrepancies of 10 percent or more in aggregate for each class
Discrepancies of 10 percent or more of total inventory value
Discrepancies that are material to the statements as a whole
why: The clause requires the auditor to report whether discrepancies of 10 percent or more in the aggregate for each class of inventory were noticed and how they were dealt with in the books. The test is applied class by class, not on total inventory.

q: A company has been sanctioned working capital limits of Rs 6 crore in aggregate from a consortium of banks on the security of current assets. Under CARO 2020 clause 3(ii)(b), the auditor must:
o: State only whether the sanctioned limits were fully utilised in the year
State whether quarterly returns filed with banks agree with the books
Report only where the sanctioned limit exceeds Rs 10 crore in total
Report only where the security is a floating charge on current assets
why: Clause 3(ii)(b) applies where working capital limits in excess of Rs 5 crore in aggregate have been sanctioned on the security of current assets, and requires comment on whether quarterly returns or statements filed with banks agree with the books. Rs 6 crore crosses the Rs 5 crore trigger.

q: Under CARO 2020 clause 3(iii), which of the following is NOT a reporting requirement in respect of loans granted?
o: Whether the terms of grant are prejudicial to the company interests
Whether repayment schedules are stipulated and repayments regular
The aggregate market value of collateral security for each loan
Whether any amount is overdue for more than ninety days at year end
why: Clause 3(iii) requires comment on prejudicial terms, stipulation and regularity of repayment schedules, amounts overdue for more than ninety days, and loans renewed or extended to settle overdues. It does not require disclosure of the market value of collateral.

q: Clause 3(iii)(f) of CARO 2020 requires the auditor to report loans or advances in the nature of loans granted:
o: Granted to any related party as defined in Section 2(76) of the Act
Repayable on demand or granted without any specified terms or period
Exceeding Rs 5 crore in aggregate to any single borrower entity
Carrying an interest rate below the prevailing bank rate of RBI
why: Clause 3(iii)(f) targets loans repayable on demand or granted without specifying any terms or period of repayment, with a separate disclosure of the aggregate amount and percentage to promoters and related parties. A low interest rate is dealt with under the prejudicial terms comment.

q: CARO 2020 clause 3(iv) deals with compliance in respect of loans, investments, guarantees and security. The relevant sections are:
o: Sections 179 and 180 on powers of the Board of Directors
Sections 185 and 186 on loans, investments and guarantees
Sections 188 and 189 on related party contracts and registers
Sections 73 to 76 on acceptance of deposits by companies
why: Clause 3(iv) requires reporting on compliance with Sections 185 and 186, dealing with loans to directors and loans, investments, guarantees and security by a company. Sections 73 to 76 relate to deposits and are covered by clause 3(v).

q: A company accepted amounts from members that are deemed deposits under the Companies Act 2013 without complying with the deposit rules. No order has been passed by any authority. Under CARO 2020 clause 3(v), the auditor should:
o: Report non-compliance with RBI directives and Sections 73 to 76
Report only if the NCLT or the Company Law Board has passed an order
Omit any comment because deemed deposits fall outside clause 3(v)
Report only the aggregate amount without commenting on compliance
why: Clause 3(v) covers deposits and amounts deemed to be deposits, and requires comment on whether the RBI directives and Sections 73 to 76 with the rules have been complied with. The clause also asks whether any order has been passed, but the absence of an order does not excuse reporting the underlying non-compliance.

q: Under CARO 2020 clause 3(vi) on cost records, the auditor is required to report whether:
o: The prescribed accounts and records have been made and maintained
The cost records have been audited and the cost audit report filed
The cost records reconcile line by line with the financials
The company employs a cost accountant in whole time employment
why: Clause 3(vi) requires the auditor to state whether the accounts and records prescribed under Section 148(1) have been made and maintained, and expressly notes that a detailed examination of such records is not required. Filing of a cost audit report is a separate compliance matter.

q: Under CARO 2020 clause 3(vii)(b), statutory dues not deposited on account of a dispute must be reported. The correct treatment is:
o: Amounts involved, the period concerned and the forum where pending
Amounts and forum only, excluding dues stayed by any court order
Only the aggregate disputed amount payable under each statute
Only where the disputed dues exceed ten percent of profit before tax
why: Clause 3(vii)(b) requires reporting the amounts involved, the period to which the amount relates and the forum where the dispute is pending, in respect of dues not deposited on account of any dispute. There is no materiality threshold built into the clause.

q: A company failed to repay a term loan instalment of Rs 2 crore to a bank on the due date and it remained unpaid at year end. It also defaulted on payment to a debenture holder. Under CARO 2020 clause 3(ix)(a), the auditor must report:
o: Only the default to the bank, since debenture holders are not lenders
Only the aggregate amount of default, without any lender-wise detail
The period and amount of default lender-wise, debenture holders included
Nothing, since the bank granted a moratorium after the balance sheet date
why: Clause 3(ix)(a) requires the auditor to report the period and amount of default in repayment of loans or other borrowings or in the payment of interest, lender-wise, and the definition of lender covers debenture holders. A post balance sheet moratorium does not erase a default existing during the year.

q: Under CARO 2020 clause 3(ix)(d), the auditor reports whether funds raised on short term basis have been utilised for long term purposes. If such utilisation is found, the auditor must:
o: Issue a qualified opinion on the financial statements of the company
Report the matter only where it raises a going concern doubt
Report the fact together with the nature and the amount involved
Report only where the amount so diverted exceeds Rs 1 crore
why: Clause 3(ix)(d) requires reporting the fact along with the nature and amount involved where short term funds have been used for long term purposes. The CARO comment is a separate statement and does not by itself modify the opinion on the financial statements.

q: CARO 2020 clause 3(xi)(a) requires reporting on fraud. The correct scope is:
o: Any fraud by the company or on the company noticed during the year
Only fraud committed by the officers or the employees of the company
Only fraud above Rs 1 crore reported to the Central Government
Only fraud established by a court or tribunal during the year
why: Clause 3(xi)(a) covers any fraud by the company or any fraud on the company that has been noticed or reported during the year, and requires the nature and the amount involved to be indicated. It is not restricted to officers and employees or to the Section 143(12) reporting threshold.

q: Under CARO 2020 clause 3(xi)(c), the auditor must state whether whistle-blower complaints received during the year have been considered. The clause applies to complaints:
o: Complaints received from employees of the company during the year
Only complaints later substantiated by the audit committee
Only where a vigil mechanism is required under Section 177(9)
Any complaints received during the year, vigil mechanism or not
why: Clause 3(xi)(c) asks whether the auditor has considered whistle-blower complaints received during the year by the company, if any. It is not conditioned on the company being required to maintain a vigil mechanism, nor on the complaint being substantiated.

q: CARO 2020 clause 3(xiv) requires comment on internal audit. The correct requirement is:
o: Whether such a system commensurate with the business size exists
Whether the internal auditor is a chartered accountant in practice
Whether the internal audit function is outsourced to an outside firm
Whether internal audit covered every branch of the company in the year
why: Clause 3(xiv) has two limbs, the existence of an internal audit system commensurate with size and nature of business, and whether the reports of the internal auditors for the period under audit were considered by the statutory auditor. The qualification and independence of the internal auditor are not the subject of this clause.

q: CARO 2020 clause 3(xviii) deals with resignation of the statutory auditor during the year. The incoming auditor must state:
o: The reasons stated in the resignation letter of the outgoing auditor verbatim
Whether the outgoing auditor filed Form ADT-3 within thirty days
Whether issues or concerns raised by the outgoing auditor were considered
Whether the resignation was approved by the audit committee of the board
why: Clause 3(xviii) requires the auditor to state whether there has been any resignation of the statutory auditors during the year and if so, whether the auditor has taken into consideration the issues, objections or concerns raised by the outgoing auditors. Form ADT-3 filing is the outgoing auditor obligation and not the subject of this comment.

q: A company has an unspent amount relating to an ongoing CSR project. Under CARO 2020 clause 3(xx)(b), the auditor reports whether the amount has been transferred to:
o: A Fund specified in Schedule VII within six months of the year end
A Fund specified in Schedule VII within thirty days of the year end
The general reserve of the company before the financial year ends
An Unspent CSR Account within thirty days under Section 135(6) of the Act
why: For ongoing projects, Section 135(6) requires the unspent amount to be transferred to an Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account within thirty days of the end of the financial year. The six month transfer to a Schedule VII Fund applies to unspent amounts other than those relating to ongoing projects and is covered by clause 3(xx)(a).
